new_statements.quote: In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed, i.e. they are pronounced with almost the same degree of prominence or force. In some languages, hovvever, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syilable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. Hovvever, it must be remembered that that is also the syilable, according to the rule mentioned earlier, vvhich is lengthened, so that the stress may be the effect of the lengthening of the vovvel. In any case, independent of the lengthening of vovvels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish vvords from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of ali Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone. [...] There are only tvvo contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low, vvhich serve to distinguish between words which are otherwise identical in ali other respects.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Country-level generalisation for 'Zambian languages': all are tone languages with two contrastive tones (H, L) on every syllable; stress is non-distinctive, syllables roughly evenly stressed, with at most slight penultimate prominence in some languages (Cewa named) attributed to penultimate vowel lengthening. Downstep in LUY, mostly restricted to KWG 3 and MWE dialects, is a result of the underlying high of the initial ... new_statements.relation_note: Two-level tone system (H, L) for all Luyana dialects incl. Nyengo; western-cluster (incl. NYE) leftward shift of stem-initial H onto the prefix, stems Low; no stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Luyana, expressly including the Nyengo (NYE) dialect, has two tonemes, High and Low; contour (falling/rising) tones and downstep occur only in a few named dialects (KWG 3-4, MUL 1, KWG 3, MBK, MWE -- Nyengo not among them). In the western cluster (Luyana West, to which Nyengo belongs per Lisimba 1982 'solid LUW (LIU, MWE, NYE, SIM)') stem syllables surface Low and the inherited stem-initial High has shifted leftward onto the prefix; this western tone-displacement innovation 'appears to originate from the NYE-MAK' area. Nothing on stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: falling tone in KWG 3-4 and MUL 1; rising tone 'extremely rare', a few examples in KWG 3 and MBK; downstep mostly restricted to KWG 3 and MWE; low-tone raising in KWG 1-3, MAS, MBK and SIM

(ch. 2: Kashoki, Mubanga E. & Michael Mann, 'A general sketch of the Bantu languages of Zambia', pp. 47-100, sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress' pp. 70-71; ch. 1 Kashoki, 'The language situation in Zambia'.) sources.quote: In Zambian languages, in contrast, syllables are more or less evenly stressed, i.e. they are pronounced with almost the same degree of prominence or force. In some languages, hovvever, (e.g. Cewa) the penultimate syilable seems to be pronounced with slightly greater force than the rest of the syllables in the same word. Hovvever, it must be remembered that that is also the syilable, according to the rule mentioned earlier, vvhich is lengthened, so that the stress may be the effect of the lengthening of the vovvel. In any case, independent of the lengthening of vovvels, stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish vvords from each other in meaning. A characteristic feature of ali Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone. [...] There are only tvvo contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low, vvhich serve to distinguish between words which are otherwise identical in ali other respects.
sources.locator: ch. 2 (Kashoki & Mann), sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress', pp. 70-71 (text-layer lines 3175-3203); Nyengo itself only at p. 19 Table 1:1 (Group C2 census row) and p. 59 Table 2:5 (Fortune 1963 lexicostatistic chart), index 'Nyengo, 19, 59'
sources.note: General statement only (Kashoki & Mann pp. 70-71): Zambian languages have even stress, possible slight penultimate prominence tied to penult lengthening, stress never distinctive; every syllable carries tone, two contrastive tones H/L, with contextual tonal alternation. No Nyengo-specific prosodic statement anywhere in the volume (Nyengo hits: p. 19 census 'Nyengo 4,608 5,591 10,199 0.3', p. 59 Table 2:5 row '79 80 79 83 84 87 89 85 84 90 Nyengo', index).
